instagram_reel.script:
People ask this all the time: can Ontario sparkling wine actually age? I just tasted a flight at i4C that answered it pretty loudly.

The 2011 wines still had energy, structure, and a whole lot of life left in them. Then the 2017s showed me three very different paths: one still finding its balance, one lovely now, and one that already feels built for the long haul.

That’s the fun part of sparkling wine. Site matters. Style matters. And patience matters too.

Canadian sparkling wine has real aging potential, and this tasting made that impossible to ignore. If you want the full breakdown, the post is up now.

linkedin.post:
A recent i4C tasting offered a useful reminder about Ontario sparkling wine: ageability is not theoretical here.

The older wines in the flight, from 2011, still had energy and structure. They were showing development, but they were far from tired. That matters, because it speaks to both the quality of the fruit and the intent behind the winemaking.

The 2017 wines were just as interesting, but for different reasons. They showed how much site and style shape the arc of a traditional method sparkling wine. Some still need time. Some are already on a clear path. One felt ready for a shorter runway.

For producers, importers, and buyers, that distinction matters. Ontario sparkling wine is not a single story. It is a range of sites, approaches, and ageing curves, and the strongest bottles are giving us a lot to talk about.

The bigger takeaway is simple: when Ontario sparkling wine is made with structure and patience in mind, it can absolutely hold its own in the conversation about age-worthy traditional method wines.
